source: Blanchette and Nipkow (2010) Nitpick: A Counterexample Generator for Higher-Order Logic Based on a Relational Model Finder (ITP 2010)
finding: Founding evaluation of Nitpick against Quickcheck and Refute on mutated Isabelle formulas (non-theorems made by swapping constants and arguments). Nitpick found genuine counterexamples on most theories at 10 s per formula; most were found within a few seconds.
numbers: 3200 random mutants, 200 from each of 20 Isabelle theories, 10 s limit. Genuine counterexamples (Quickcheck G/X on executable mutants; Refute and Nitpick G +potential): Map 43/62 vs 0+0 vs 157+0; Fun 5/9 vs 162+1 vs 163+0; Predicate 19/34 vs 103+45 vs 161+0; Divides 134/184 vs 3+15 vs 141+2; List 119/162 vs 1+17 vs 117+9; ArrowGS 0/0 vs 0+126 vs 139+2. Nitpick weaker on MacLaurin (26+7 vs Refute 3+113), CoreC++ (29+1), Ordinal (12+0).
limits: Mutants are a proxy; the authors say no database of real non-theorems existed. Refute counts are mostly potential (possibly spurious) because of its unsound three-valued logic, so the comparison favours Nitpick partly by definition. Weak on real arithmetic and large state spaces. No LLM involved.
agent_relevance: A finite-model search over small scopes finds refutations in seconds for most small algebraic and datatype claims. Gives a cost anchor for an S7 tool call: seconds, not minutes. Real arithmetic and large state spaces are where it fails, so route only suitable claims.

source: Blanchette and Nipkow (2010) Nitpick, TPTP higher-order model-finding run (same paper, section 7)
finding: In a preliminary run on the higher-order model-finding division of TPTP, Nitpick disproved more formulas than Refute and exposed soundness bugs in provers.
numbers: Nitpick disproved 293 of 2729 formulas (mostly theorems, so most cannot be falsified) vs 214 for Refute. Nitpick produced counterexamples for 5 formulas previously 'proved' by TPS or LEO-II, revealing 2 bugs in TPS and 1 in LEO-II.
quote: Nitpick exhibited counterexamples for five formulas that had previously been proved by TPS or LEO-II
limits: Preliminary run; no timeout stated in the text I read. The 2729 are mostly valid, so 293 is a hit count, not a rate on false formulas. Same paper as d01, not independent.
agent_relevance: A model finder is also a checker of provers: a found model is a certificate that can catch wrong proofs. Supports using a countermodel as an independent check on the agent's own confident derivation.

source: Reynolds, Tinelli, Goel, Krstic, Deters, Barrett (2017) Constraint Solving for Finite Model Finding in SMT Solvers (TPLP)
finding: Head-to-head on satisfiable TPTP problems (the problems where a countermodel exists). Paradox, a MACE-style finder, solved the most. The SMT model finder in CVC4 was behind overall but ahead on equality-heavy problems.
numbers: TPTP 5.4.0, unsorted first-order, 300 s per problem. Paradox 1450 satisfiable problems (best). cvc4+fm 1277, cvc4+f 1190, cvc4+fmi 1165, z3 941. CVC4 configurations together solved 52 satisfiable problems Paradox did not and 36 that iProver finite-model mode did not. On the SEQ class (some equality) cvc4 solved 214 more than Paradox. Authors credit Paradox's lead to clause splitting and sort inference.
limits: Authors are the CVC4 team. Totals are counts of satisfiable problems solved; the denominator was not in the lines I read. Different tools win on different problem classes.
agent_relevance: No single finder dominates; a portfolio (Paradox plus an SMT finder) adds coverage, as K04 says for strategies. Gives the Paradox number for gap 6 under a 300 s limit.

source: Baumgartner, Fuchs, de Nivelle, Tinelli (2009) Computing finite models by reduction to function-free clause logic (J. Applied Logic): FM-Darwin vs Mace4 vs Paradox
finding: Direct comparison of Mace4 and Paradox 1.3 on all satisfiable TPTP problems. Paradox clearly beat Mace4. Mace4 failed by timeout on 169 problems and by memory on others that FM-Darwin solved.
numbers: TPTP 3.1.1, 1251 satisfiable problems, 300 s CPU, 512 MB, default settings. Paradox 1083, FM-Darwin 1074, Mace4 802. The solved sets are neither subsets nor supersets of each other. FM-Darwin solves 328 problems Mace4 cannot (169 Mace4 timeouts, the rest out of memory) and 82 that Paradox cannot.
limits: One author wrote Darwin. Old versions (Mace4 2003 era, Paradox 1.3). These are not the CASC reports; the CASC model-finding track tables were not obtained (search quota ran out). MACE 1994 original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Mace4 solves about 64 percent (802/1251) and Paradox about 87 percent (1083/1251) of satisfiable TPTP problems at 300 s. If the agent calls a finite-model tool, a Paradox-style finder is the stronger default; Mace4 misses about 1 in 3 satisfiable problems.

source: Zouak et al. (2026) Counterexample Generation via Per-Theorem Symbolic Verifiers: When Imitation Hurts and Reinforcement Repairs (arXiv 2610.02444)
finding: An exact Python verifier per theorem (checks every remaining hypothesis and the negated conclusion) scored and trained the model. With the verifier as reward, a 4B model rose from 0.30 to 0.50 greedy pass@1 on false claims and passed every 7B math model tested.
numbers: SymCE: 4,707 false undergraduate algebra and analysis conjectures made by dropping a hypothesis from 6,748 theorems; held-out n=201. Qwen3-4B base 0.30 [0.24,0.37]; SFT 0.35 [0.28,0.41] (paired delta CI [-0.030,+0.119], not significant); RLVR 0.50 [0.43,0.57] (paired delta +0.199 [+0.13,+0.27]); four-seed means 0.49 +/-0.02 dense, 0.46 +/-0.03 sparse. Best 7B (Eurus-2-7B-PRIME) 0.30 [0.24,0.36]. Six DeepSeek/Gemini APIs 0.42 to 0.58. Pass@8: RLVR 0.68, base 0.49.
limits: Training study, not a prompting test; says nothing about tool use at inference. Synthetic hypothesis-dropping claims, one-line Python witnesses, 4B model. Frontier API rows are only a range. The verifiers were built with an LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro) then audited (d07).
agent_relevance: The falsification gap can be attacked with an exact, fast check (tens of milliseconds). S7 should run a witness through code that tests each hypothesis and the negated conclusion before any refutation is accepted. Bears on gap 2 and gap 8.

source: Zouak et al. (2026) SymCE, imitation-trap result (same paper as d05)
finding: Training only on counterexamples makes the model emit witnesses for true statements. Recognition of true theorems fell from 0.27 to 0.00 after counterexample-only SFT, in all four seeds and on Gemma-3-4B. Sparse-reward RL repaired it. A leading invalid kind: hypotheses satisfied but the conclusion not actually negated.
numbers: True-theorem pass@1: base 0.27, SFT 0.00, dense RL 0.34, sparse RL 0.65. Explicit true/false classification: base 0.36, SFT 0.21, dense 0.73, sparse 0.84. Under SFT the 'hypotheses ok, conclusion not negated' failure rose from 1 to 31 percent. Abstention: 0 percent SFT, 2 percent dense, 10 percent sparse. Dense and sparse tie in-domain but differ by about 33 points on a held-out calibration probe.
limits: Same paper as d05, not independent. Small model, narrow domain; calibration probe is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Data for gap 2: a model pushed to always find a counterexample produces many invalid ones, mainly by not checking the negated conclusion. Rule for S7: 'no counterexample found' must stay a legal output; never accept a witness without the negated-conclusion check.

source: Zouak et al. (2026) SymCE, verifier audit (same paper as d05)
finding: The exact checker is itself not perfect: a human audit of its decisions found a few errors.
numbers: 177 verifier decisions audited by humans; 97.7 percent accurate (about 4 wrong).
limits: Audit sample of 177 on real policy outputs; the error types are in an appendix I did not read.
agent_relevance: An exact checker removes most but not all invalid counterexamples. About 2 percent residual with code checking; use a second check when stakes are high.

source: Deng et al. (2026) Beyond the Verdict: Agentic Code Judging with Verifiable Feedback (ARBITER, arXiv 2610.18760)
finding: RL training of a 35B agent in a code sandbox, where a counterexample must be a legal input the candidate fails on (checked by the official checker), raised counterexample success on wrong programs from 40.61 to 62.67 percent and verdict accuracy from 71.41 to 87.41 percent.
numbers: USACO-JUDGE (USACO 2026 contests) and UOJ-Bench hacking splits. Same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone: overall hack success 40.61 to 62.67; hard-split verdict accuracy 67.43 to 83.40 (UOJ) and 65.34 to 84.50 (USACO-JUDGE). One ARBITER sample beat eight no-tool samples on every split.
limits: Table 1 extraction was column-scrambled, so only abstract and prose numbers are used. Code only. Training, not prompting.
agent_relevance: A trained critic can raise real refutation rate on plausible-but-wrong code, with execution as arbiter. Supports gap 8 for code; says nothing about natural-language reasoning.

source: Deng et al. (2026) ARBITER human audit and ablation (same paper as d08)
finding: Whether the executed counterexample succeeds tracks whether the written diagnosis is right. Giving the repair model the diagnosis helps; adding the counterexample generator source gives no consistent extra gain.
numbers: 400 ARBITER diagnoses audited by three competitive programmers (initial labels agreed on all 400). Among compilable candidates counterexamples succeed for 71.6 percent of correct diagnoses vs 10.3 percent of incorrect or vacuous ones. Of 163 correct diagnoses naming a real bug, 82.2 percent locate the cause and 54.0 percent suggest a fix. At Best@8 verdict plus diagnosis beats online-judge feedback at every difficulty tier for both solvers.
limits: Audit is on one model's output. The IOI 2026 case study numbers were not checked.
agent_relevance: A failing input is a cheap proxy for a right diagnosis: about 7 in 10 when a test fails, about 1 in 10 when none does. Use test result as the gate on trusting a written critique. Bears on gap 7: diagnosis, not only the failing input, drives repair.

source: Jenne, Brown, He, Kvinge (2026) Beyond Selected Breakthroughs: Evaluating Language Models on Randomly Sampled Mathematical Conjectures (OpenConjecture, arXiv 2610.40382)
finding: Three passes of frontier GPT models on 200 random arXiv conjectures. Counterexamples were reviewed only by another instance of the same model; many exploit a missing hypothesis or odd reading. No expert review was done, so the share that survives as non-trivial is not measured.
numbers: Candidate solutions for about 60 percent of 200 conjectures; 70 got counterexamples, 55 proofs; 84 percent of proposed resolutions passed an LLM review. Of verified counterexamples from passes 1 and 2, about 60 percent were rated off-the-shelf and the rest standard construction; most pass-3 counterexamples were nontrivial modification (5 of 6). Examples: trivial group, 5-cycle, complete graph on 5 vertices, single-vertex graph. Some responses carry a Scope paragraph listing amendments that remove the counterexample.
limits: Authors say they did not attempt expert verification. Reviewer is the same model family as the solver. Novelty labels are model judgments. A check-intended-hypotheses step was not tested as an intervention.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 only half answered: about 60 percent of early counterexamples are textbook-standard and a notable share lean on imprecise statements. S7 should ask whether a counterexample lies inside the intended domain and mark literal-only ones weak. No measured gain from that step yet.

source: Li, Li, Yang, Ma, Su (2026) Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with Large Language Models (arXiv 2603.19514 v2; marked rejected from ICLR 2026)
finding: Training on 575K hypothesis-dropping mutations of Lean 4 theorems, with Lean as exact checker, raised formal counterexample pass@1 well above the strongest baseline. Same direction as CounterMath fine-tuning, independent group.
numbers: FOR-COUNTER (1,058 problems, CounterMath-source books formalized with Kimina-Autoformalizer): problems solved pass@1 ours 222 vs strongest baseline 127; pass@4 274 vs 200; pass@9 302 vs 224. General-purpose LLMs solve far fewer at pass@1 (about 19 to 30 in the rows I could read). Validation pass@1 49.8 percent vs 43 percent for the single-reward ablation. Reported relative gain 47 to 74 percent over the strongest baseline at pass@1 on three benchmarks.
limits: Authors give counts not rates because the benchmark has autoformalization errors. Marked rejected from ICLR 2026. Formal witnesses need a Lean proof, a far stricter bar than informal counterexamples. Table row labels are scrambled in my extraction, so baseline names are not given.
agent_relevance: Confirms the K23 numbers (127 to 222) from the primary paper. With exact formal checking invalid counterexamples are ruled out, at the price of missing valid informal ones: precision for recall. Bears on gap 2.

source: Wang, Kuang, Li et al. (2026) INSPIRE: An Internalize-Then-Improve Approach for Example-Driven Mathematical Reasoning (arXiv 2608.27501)
finding: A second, independent counterexample-training paper tests out-of-distribution transfer and finds small, mostly flat gains. This weakens the CounterMath out-of-distribution headline (AIME 20 to 30).
numbers: CounterMath F1: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct 38.67 to 45.91 (full pipeline); 1.5B model reaches 39.02 vs 7B base 38.67. OOD for 7B: GSM8K 94.54 to 95.68, MATH500 84.20 to 84.80 (+0.6, 3 of 500 problems), AIME 2024 13.33 to 20.00 (+6.67, 2 of 30 problems), MMLU college math 72 to 75. For Llama-8B and the 1.5B model AIME 2024 is unchanged (6.67; 10.00); MATH500 +1.8 and +1.2. SFT alone F1 +0.39. Plain DPO lowered example use (77.63 to 73.19).
limits: Single runs with fixed seeds, no confidence intervals (authors say so). Judge is DeepSeek-V3.2, cross-checked with GPT-4o. Not a replication of the CounterMath fine-tune itself (different method and data).
agent_relevance: Gap 9 mostly closed in the negative: OOD gains from counterexample training are within noise on AIME and about 1 point on MATH500. Do not count on counterexample training as a general reasoning booster.

source: Arjomandbigdeli, Zhou, Bak (2026) Large Language Models as Falsifiers for Cyber-Physical Systems (LLM-Falsifier, arXiv 2609.20752)
finding: An LLM used as the search engine for counterexamples to formal specs (given signal names, trajectories and critical-time witnesses) ranked first on 14 of 21 ARCH-COMP specifications by mean simulations, with a uniform random baseline in the same table. It also failed completely on some specs where an optimizer succeeded.
numbers: 10 runs per spec. On 6 specs the LLM falsified in one simulation in every run. AT1: LLM 1.0 simulations vs FReaK 4.8 (random found 0 of 10). AT51 and AT54: LLM 0 of 10 found, FReaK 10 of 10. One NN spec: LLM 1 of 10 vs FReaK 10 of 10. CC4: LLM 5 of 10 vs FReaK 10 of 10. Prompt ablation MP1 to MP4: more semantic context mostly improves, MP4 best. Larger model with more reasoning (gpt-5-mini high) found more with fewer simulations than gpt-5-nano low or gpt-oss-20b low.
limits: Metric is simulation count, not tokens. Numeric cyber-physical search, not logic claims. LLM cost not counted. Authors say the falsification rate may be underestimated in the tables.
agent_relevance: Partial support for gaps 1 and 5: LLM semantic search and numeric optimizers win on different specs, which supports a union of strategies. Not equal-token.

source: Kato (2026) GTDD: Generative Test-Driven Development for AI Coding Agents with Adversarial Testing (arXiv 2610.02952)
finding: Paired experiment on a stateful key-value store (30 blocks, 150 trajectories, four rounds). Regenerating tests after each candidate lowered the final failure rate vs one fixed LLM-written test set, but a random property-based generator was as good, and showing the tester the candidate's source added nothing.
numbers: Failure rate after round 4. Dynamic informed minus Static LLM -0.131 [-0.228,-0.050], p=0.0015 (lower in 19 blocks, higher in 7). Dynamic informed minus Dynamic blind -0.005 [-0.044,+0.034], p=0.81. Dynamic informed minus Static property -0.024 [-0.097,+0.043], p=0.53. Static property minus Static LLM -0.107 [-0.205,-0.018], p=0.029. 37.2 percent of valid traces fail the current module (informed), 35.7 (blind). Only 1 of 150 trajectories reached failure rate <= 0.01. Equal-trace controls (Static LLM 600: 0.355; Blind rerun: 0.308) not significantly different.
limits: One system, one LLM family, wide intervals. The equal-count conditions did not isolate which feature caused the gain. The property generator comes from the spec that built the evaluation set, so it is a strong baseline.
agent_relevance: For gap 5: at equal test counts a cheap random property generator matched LLM-adaptive testing, so the union gain over a random arm may be small on well-specified code. S7 should always include a random/property arm as a floor. Also bears on gap 4: source access (more information for design) gave no gain.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Two-Stage Reinforcement Learning for Sound and Adversarial Test Generation in Code LLMs (TCS, arXiv 2609.03955)
finding: Training a model to write counterexample-style tests in two stages (sound tests first, then tests aimed at current failure modes) improves pass@1 and test-based selection. Self-generated tests help but curated public tests alone are still better.
numbers: LiveCodeBench, 7B base: pass@1 28.56 to 43.01 with self-generated-test selection at BoN-32. Public tests alone 45.99; public plus self-generated 46.15.
limits: Training study on code; figures from the prose of section 5, Table 1 not parsed. Single paper.
agent_relevance: For gap 8 and K07: generated adversarial tests are a useful selector but not a replacement for trusted tests (28.56 to 43.01 vs 45.99 curated). Soundness of the test matters as much as sharpness.

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning (arXiv 2305.12295)
finding: The only controlled test I could open of LLM plus external logic solver (Prover9, Z3, others) vs LLM alone. It is not a counterexample study (the solvers prove or fail), but it measures the translate-then-solve gain and cost. On GPT-4 the solver helps on 4 of 5 datasets but hurts on PrOntoQA, where chain of thought is already 98.8.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy Standard / CoT / Logic-LM (no refinement): PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20; ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04. GPT-3.5 chat ProofWriter 35.50 / 49.17 / 58.33. Executable rate of the translation (text-davinci-003): FOLIO 79.9, AR-LSAT 32.6 percent. When translation fails the system falls back on CoT.
limits: No token-matched control; Logic-LM adds calls. Not about refutation. 2023 models. Does not isolate countermodel finding.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open for counterexamples, but the pattern is clear: a solver gives big gains where the claim translates cleanly (ProofWriter +11.5 over CoT with GPT-4) and loses where translation fails. A finite-model or SMT call in S7 pays only when the claim can be written formally.
